questions.question:
A photon and an electron, each of \(20~\text{eV}\) energy, move in free space. The ratio of the linear momentum of electron \(p_\mathrm{e}\) to that of photon \(p_\mathrm{ph},\) \(\dfrac {p_\mathrm{e}}{p_\mathrm{ph}}\)is:
(take speed of light \(=3\times10^8~\text{ms}^{-1}, \) charge of electron \(=-1.6\times 10^{-19}~\text{C}\) and mass of electron \(=9 \times 10^{-31}~\text{kg}\))
1. \(275\) 2. \(\dfrac {2 } {450}\)
3. \(\dfrac {1} {250}\) 4. \(225\)
questions.explanation:
Hint: \(P_{ph} = \dfrac{E}{c}, P_{e} = \sqrt{2mE}\)

Step: Find the ratio of the linear momentum of the electron \((p_{e})\) to that of photon \((p_{ph})\).
The momentum of the photon is given by;
\(p_{ph} = \dfrac{E}{c}\)
 The momentum of the electron is given by;
\(p_{e} = \sqrt{2mE}\)
 The ratio of the linear momentum of the electron \((p_{e})\) to that of photon \((p_{ph})\)  is given by;
\(\dfrac{p_e}{p_{ph}}= c\sqrt{\dfrac{2m}{E}}\)
\(\Rightarrow \dfrac{p_e}{p_{ph}}= 3\times 10^{8}\sqrt{\dfrac{2\times 9\times 10^{-31}}{20\times 1.6\times 10^{-19}}}\)
\(\Rightarrow \dfrac{p_e}{p_{ph}}= 225\)
Hence, option (4) is the correct answer.

questions.question:
Water flows in a streamline motion through a horizontal pipe of circular cross-section, as shown in the figure. The pressure difference of water between \(P\) and \(Q\) is \(15~\text{Nm}^{-2}.\) The areas of cross-section at \(P\) and \(Q\) are \(40~\text{cm}^2\) and \(20~\text{cm}^2,\) respectively. The rate of flow of water through the pipe, in \(\text{cm}^{3} \text{s}^{-1},\) is:
(take the density of water\(=1000~\text{kg}~\text{m}^{-3}\))
1. \(400\) 2. \(100\)
3. \(200\) 4. \(300\)
questions.explanation:
Hint: \(A_1v_1 = A_2 v_2\)

Step: Find the rate of flow of water through the pipe.
Given: \(P_{P}- P_{Q} = 15~\text{Nm}^{-2}, \rho =10^{3}~\text{kg m}^{-3}, A_{P} = 40~\text{m}^2, A_{Q} = 20~\text{m}^2\)
According to Continuity equation;
\(A_{P}v_{P} = A_{Q}v_{Q}\)
\(\Rightarrow v_{Q} = \dfrac{A_{P}}{A_{Q}}v_{P}\)
\(\Rightarrow v_{Q} = 2v_{P}~~~...(1)\)
By applying Bernoulli's equation we get;
Since the pipe is horizontal,
\(P_{P} + \dfrac{1}{2}\rho v_{P}^2 = P_{Q} + \dfrac{1}{2}\rho v_{Q}^2\)
\(\Rightarrow P_{P} + \dfrac{1}{2}\rho v_{P}^2 = P_{Q} + \dfrac{1}{2}\rho v_{Q}^2\)
\(\Rightarrow P_{P} -P_{Q} = \dfrac{1}{2}\rho(v_{Q}^2-v_{P}^2)\)
\(\Rightarrow 15= \dfrac{1}{2}10^{3}((2v_{P})^2-v_{P}^2)\)
\(\Rightarrow 30= 10^{3}(3v_{P}^2)\)
\(\Rightarrow v^2_{P} = \dfrac{1}{100}\)
\(\Rightarrow v_{P} = \dfrac{1}{10}= 0.1~\text{m/s} = 10~\text{cm/s}\)
The rate of the flow of water through the pipe is given by;
\(Q = A_{P}v_{P} = 40 \times 10 = 400~\text{cm}^{3}\text{s}^{-1}\)
Hence, option (1) is the correct answer.

questions.question:
A thin horizontal disc is rotating about a vertical axis passing through its fixed centre \(O.\) Its angular momentum is \(L_A\) and \(L_B\) computed about points \(A\) and \(B,\) respectively, with \(OB =2 \times OA.\) The value of \(\dfrac{L_A}{L_B}\) is:
1. \(2\) 2. \(\dfrac{1}{4}\)
3. \(\dfrac{1}{2}\) 4. \(1\)
questions.explanation:
Hint: \(L = I\omega\)

Step: Find the value of the ratio of \(\dfrac{L_{A}}{L_{B}}\).
For a rigid body, the angular momentum about any point \(P\) is given by;
\(L_{P} = L_{CM} + \vec r_{CM/P}\times M \vec V_{CM}\)
Where \(CM \) is the centre of mass
As the disc rotates about a fixed centre \(O\), so, the centre of mass is at \(O\), and \(\vec V_{CM} =0\)
Therefore, for any point \(P \), \(\vec r_{CM/P}\times M \vec V_{CM} =0\).
\(\Rightarrow L_A = L_{O}, L_{B} = L_{O}\)
So the angular momentum is the same about every point.
Therefore, the value of the ratio of \(\dfrac{L_{A}}{L_{B}}\)  is \(1\).
Hence, option (4) is the correct answer.

questions.question:
Consider a long solenoid of length \(l\) and radius \(r.\) If \(n\) is the number of turns per unit length and \( \mu_0 \) is the permeability of free space, the inductance of the solenoid is:
1. \(2\mu_0 \pi n^2 r^2 l\)
2. \(\mu_0 \pi n^2 r^2 l\)
3. \(\mu_0 n^2 r^2 l\)
4. \((\mu_0/2 \pi)n^2r^2l\)
questions.explanation:
Hint: \(L = \dfrac{\mu_0 N^2 A}{l} = \mu_0 n^2 Al\)

Step: Find the inductance of the solenoid.
The magnetic field inside the solenoid is given by;
\(B = \mu_0 nI\)
The area of the single turn is given by;
\(A = \pi r^2\)
The magnetic flux through a single turn is given by;
\(\phi = BA = \mu_0 nI \times \pi r^2\)
Since there are \(N=nl\) turns,
\(\phi = \mu_0 n^2 I \pi r^2 l\)
By the definition of the inductance, we get;
\(L = \dfrac{\phi}{I} = \dfrac{\mu_0 n^2 I\pi r^2 l}{I} = \mu_0 n^2 \pi r^2 l\)
Hence, option (2) is the correct answer.

questions.question:
The temperature of a metallic sphere of radius \(R\) is increased by a small amount \(\Delta T.\) If the linear coefficient of thermal expansion of the metal is \(\alpha,\) the approximate increase in the volume of the sphere is:
1. \(6\pi R^3 \alpha \Delta T\)
2. \(2\pi R^3 \alpha \Delta T\)
3. \(3\pi R^3 \alpha \Delta T\)
4. \(4\pi R^3 \alpha \Delta T\)
questions.explanation:
Hint: \(\dfrac{\Delta V}{V} = 3\dfrac{\Delta R}{R}, \Delta R = R \alpha \Delta T\)

Step: Find the increase in the volume of the sphere.
The volume of the sphere is \(V = \dfrac{4}{3}\pi R^3\)
For a small increase in temperature \(\Delta T\), \(R' = R_0 (1+ \alpha \Delta T)\)
The new volume of the sphere is given by;
\(V' = \dfrac{4}{3}\pi R'^{3}= \dfrac{4}{3}\pi R^{3}(1+ \alpha \Delta T)^3\) 
Using the approximation \((1+ x)^3\approx 1+3x~~~~~~~[x<<<1]\)
\(V' = \dfrac{4}{3}\pi R^{3} (1+ 3\alpha \Delta T)\)
\(\Rightarrow V' = \dfrac{4}{3}\pi R^{3} + 4\pi R^3\alpha \Delta T\)
\(\Rightarrow V' -V = 4\pi R^3\alpha \Delta T\)
\(\Rightarrow \Delta V = 4\pi R^3\alpha \Delta T\)
Hence, option (4) is the correct answer.

questions.question:
Consider two circuits, \((\mathrm{A})\) and \((\mathrm{B}),\) each having two resistors. One of them has a positive temperature coefficient of resistance, \(+\alpha\), while the other one has a negative temperature coefficient of resistance, \(-\alpha\), as shown in the figure. The currents through these circuits are denoted by \(I_A\) and \(I_B\). At the initial temperature, the resistance of the two resistors is \(R_0.\) As the temperature is increased, the correct option that describes the variation of current in these circuits is:   

1. both \(I_A\) and \(I_B\) remain constant
2. \(I_A\) remains constant while \(I_B\) increases
3. \(I_A\) decreases while \(I_B\) increases
4. \(I_A\) increases while \(I_B\) decreases
questions.explanation:
Hint: Recall series and parallel combination of resistance. 

Step: Find the correct relation of the current in the circuits. 
We know that, resistance of the conductor varies with temperature i.e., \(R_t = R_0 (1+ \alpha \Delta T) \).
For negative temperature coefficient, \(R_1 = R_0 (1- \alpha \Delta T) \)
For positive temperature coefficient, \(R_2= R_0 (1+\alpha \Delta T) \)
For the series combination, the equivalent resistance of the circuit is given by;
\(R_{eq} = R_1 + R_2 = R_0 (1- \alpha \Delta T) + R_0 (1+ \alpha \Delta T) = 2R_0\)
So, in the equivalent resistance the temperature-dependent terms cancel exactly.
The current in the circuit is given by; 
\(I_A = \dfrac{V}{2R_0}\)
So, the current is independent of temperature.
In parallel combination, \(R_{eq} = \dfrac{R_1R_2}{R_1 +R_2}= \dfrac{R^2_0 (1-\alpha^2\Delta T^2)}{2R_0}= \dfrac{R_0 (1-\alpha^2\Delta T^2)}{2}\)
Since, \(1-\alpha^2\Delta T^2<0\)
for any nonzero \(\Delta T\), the equivalent resistance decreases as temperature increases.
The current in the circuit is given by;
\(I_B= \dfrac{2V}{R_0(1-\alpha^2\Delta T^2)}\)
So, the current is increases with temperature.
Therefore,  \(I_A\) remains constant while \(I_B\) increases
Hence, option (2) is the correct answer.

questions.question:
An ideal Zener diode with a breakdown voltage of \(-3~\text{V}\) is reverse-biased with a negative input voltage \(V_i=-5~\text{V}.\) The magnitude of the voltage difference between points \(B\) and \(A\) is:

1. \(0\) V 
2. \(3\) V
3. \(2\) V 
4. \(1\) V
questions.explanation:
Hint: Apply Kirchhoff's voltage loop.

Step: Find the  magnitude of the voltage difference between points \(B\) and \(A\) .
Given: Ideal Zener diode with breakdown voltage \(V_Z = -3~\text{V}\), applied input voltage \(V_i =-5~\text{V}\)
Since the reverse voltage applied is \(|-5~\text{V}|= 5~\text{V}> 3~\text{V}\), the Zener diode goes into reverse breakdown. Hence, the voltage across the Zener diode is fixed at \(V_Z = 3~\text{V}\).
The total applied voltage is \(5~\text{V}\), out of this, \(3~\text{V}\) appears across the Zener diode. Therefore, the remaining voltage across the resistor (between points \(A\) and \(B\)) is \(V_{AB} = 5-3 =2~\text{V}\).
Hence, option (3) is the correct answer.

Two planets \(P_1\) and \(P_2\) with equal mass have radii \(R_1\) and \(R_2,\) respectively, where \(R_2=\dfrac{R_1}{2}.\) The escape speeds of \(P_1\) and \(P_2 \) are \(v_1\) and \(v_2,\) respectively. Then \(\dfrac {v_2}{v_1}\) is:
1. \(2\) 2. \( \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\)
3. \(1\) 4. \(\sqrt{2}\)
questions.explanation:
Hint: \(v= \sqrt{2gR}\)

Step: Find the ratio of escape velocity \(\dfrac {v_2}{v_1}\).
The escape speed from a planet is given by;
\(v_e = \sqrt{\dfrac{2GM}{R}}\)
Since both planets have equal mass,
\(v_{e}\propto \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{R}}\)
\(\Rightarrow \dfrac{v_2}{v_1} = \sqrt{\dfrac{R_1}{R_2}} \)
\(\Rightarrow \dfrac{v_2}{v_1} = \sqrt{2}~~~~~~~~\left[R_2 = \dfrac{R_1}{2}\right]\)

An ac voltage\(V=220~\mathrm{sin} (2 \times 10^3t)\) Volt is applied to a series \(LCR\) circuit. Then the current amplitude in the circuit is: (given: \(L=10~ \text{mH},\) \(C=25~\mu \text{F},\) \(R=100~\Omega\))
1. \(22.0\) A 2. \(2.2\) A
3. \(5.5\) A 4. \(11.0\) A
questions.explanation:
Hint: \(I = \dfrac{V}{Z}, Z = \sqrt{R^2 + (X_L-X_C)^2}\)

Step: Find the current amplitude in the circuit. 
The  ac voltage \(V=220~\mathrm{sin} (2 \times 10^3t)\) Volt
The voltage amplitude is given by; \(V_0 = 220 ~\text{V}\) and angular frequency \(\omega= 2\times 10^{3}~\text{rad/s}\).
\(L = 10~\text{mH} = 0.01~\text{H}, C = 25~\mu\text{F}, R = 100~\Omega\)
\(X_L = \omega L = 2\times 10^{3}\times 0.01 = 20~\Omega \)
\(X_C = \dfrac{1}{\omega C}= \dfrac{1}{2\times 10^{3}\times 25\times 10^{-6}} = 20~\Omega \)
\(\Rightarrow X_L = X_C\)
The circuit is in resonance, so the impedance is;
\(Z= R = 100~\Omega\)
The current amplitude in the circuit is given by;
\(I = \dfrac{V_0}{R}\)
\(\Rightarrow I = \dfrac{220}{100}= 2.2~\text{A}\)
Hence, option (2) is the correct answer.

questions.question:
Two identical inductors are connected in two different configurations, \(P\) and \(Q,\) where a time-varying current \(I(t)\) is flowing, as shown in the figure. The induced EMF between points \(a\) and \(b\) for configuration \(P\) is \(E_P\) and that for configuration \(Q\) is \(E_Q.\) The ratio \(E_P/E_Q\) is:
(Neglect the effect of mutual inductance.)
1. \(2\) 2. \(1/4\)
3. \(1/2\) 4. \(1\)
questions.explanation:
Hint: \(\varepsilon= -L\dfrac{dI}{dt}\)

Step: Find the ratio of energy \(\dfrac{E_P}{E_Q}\).
Let the self-inductance of each identical inductor be \(L\). The induced emf across an inductor is \(E= L\dfrac{dI}{dt}\).
Two identical inductors are in series, so the same current \(I(t)\) flows through both. The point \(b\) is the junction between the inductors, so the emf between \(a\) and \(b\) is just the emf across the upper inductor:
\(E_P= L\dfrac{dI}{dt}\)
In configuration, \(Q\)
The two inductors are connected in parallel between \(a\) and \(b\). 
The equivalent inductance, \(L_{eq} = \dfrac{L}{2}\)
The total current is \(I(t)\), so by symmetry each branch carries \(\dfrac{I}{2}\). 
Hence, the current through each inductor changes at the rate \(\dfrac{1}{2}\dfrac{dI}{dt}\). The voltage across each parallel branch (and hence between   \(a\) and \(b\) ) is 
\(E_Q=\dfrac{ L}{2}\dfrac{dI}{dt}\)
The ratio of the energy \(\dfrac{E_P}{E_Q} = 2\).
Hence, option (1) is the correct answer.

questions.question:
Three identical capacitors, \(P,\) \(Q\) and \(S,\) each of the capacitance \(C,\) are connected to a battery of voltage \(V,\) as shown in the figure. If the energy stored in the capacitor \(P\) and total energy stored in the system are \(U_P\) and \(U_T,\) respectively, then the ratio \(\dfrac {U_P}{U_T}\)  is:

1. \(1/6\)
2. \(2/3\)
3. \(1/3\)
4. \(1/2\)
questions.explanation:
Hint: \(U = \dfrac{1}{2}CV^2\)

Step: Find the ratio of the \(\dfrac{U_P}{U_T}\).
From figure, capacitors \(P\) and \(Q\) are in series and series combination is in parallel with capacitor \(S\). The entire parallel combination is connected across the battery of voltage \(V\). 
Since \(P\) and \(Q\) are identical and in series, the applied voltage \(V\) divides equally i.e., \(V_{P} = \dfrac{V}{2}\).
The energy stored in the capacitor \(P\) is given by;
\(U_{P} = \dfrac{1}{2}C \left(\dfrac{V}{2}\right)^2 = \dfrac{CV^2}{8}\)
The parallel combination of the capacitors \(P\) and \(Q\) is given by;
\(C_{PQ} = \dfrac{C}{2}\)
The equivalent capacitance of the circuit is given by;
\(C_{eq} = \dfrac{C}{2}+ C = \dfrac{3C}{2}\)
The total energy stored in the capacitor is given by;
\(U_{T} = \dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{3C}{2}\right) V^2 = \dfrac{3CV^2}{4}\)
The required ratio is given by;
\(\dfrac{U_{P}}{U_{T}}= \dfrac{1}{6}\)
Hence, option (1) is the correct answer.

questions.question:
In an adiabatic expansion, the temperature of one mole of an ideal monatomic gas \(\left ( \gamma =5/3 \right )\) decreases from \(60~\text{K}\) to \(50~\text{K}.\) The work done by the gas in the process is:
(take the universal gas constant as \(R=8.31\) mol-1 K-1)
1. \(166\) J
2. \(41.5\) J
3. \(83.1\) J
4. \(124.5\) J
questions.explanation:
Hint: \(W = \dfrac{nR(T_2 -T_1)}{\gamma-1}\)

Step: Find the work done by the gas.
For an adiabatic process, heat exchanged, \(Q=0\). From the first law of thermodynamics \(dQ = dU + dW\)
\(\Rightarrow dU = -dW\)
For \(1\) mole of a monatomic ideal gas,
\(C_V = \dfrac{3R}{2}\)
The change in internal energy is given by;
\(dU = nC_V \Delta T\)
\(\Rightarrow dU = \dfrac{3R}{2}(T_2-T_1)\)
\(\Rightarrow dU = \dfrac{3R}{2}(50-60)= -15R\)
\(\Rightarrow dW= -dU = 15\times 8.31 = 124.65~\text{J}\approx 124.5~\text{J}\)
Hence, option (4) is the correct answer.

questions.question:
Consider a particle moving along a straight line, whose position as a function of time is given by; \(s(t)=\alpha t^2 - \beta t + \gamma,\)   where \(\alpha = 1 \text{ ms}^{-2},\) \(\beta = 6 \text{ ms}^{-1}\)  and \(\gamma = 5 \text{ m}.\) The average speed of the particle, in \(\text{ms}^{-1}\), from \(t=0\) to \(t=6\) s is:
1. \(0\)
2. \(12\)
3. \(6\)
4. \(3\)
questions.explanation:
Hint: \(v_{avg} = \dfrac{1}{t_2-t_1}\int^{t_2}_{t_1} v(t) dt\)

Step: Find the average speed of the particle.
The position of the particle as a function of time is given by;
\(s(t)=\alpha t^2 - \beta t + \gamma\)
\(\Rightarrow s(t)= t^2 -6t+5\)
The velocity of the particle is given by;
\(v(t) = \dfrac{ds}{dt} = 2t-6\)
Given: \(v =0\)
\(\Rightarrow 2t-6= 0\)
\(\Rightarrow t=3~\text{s}\)
Thus, the particle changes direction at \(t= 3~\text{s}\).
At \(t=0 ~\text{s}\), \(s(0) = 5~\text{m}\)
At \(t=3 ~\text{s}\), \(s(3) = 9-18+5= -4~\text{m}\)

\(dW = f_{k}(x) dx= (\mu_0-\alpha x)Mgdx\)
Hence, the total work done by friction from \(x=0\) to \(x=L\) is
\(W= Mg\int^{L}_{0} (\mu_0-\alpha x)dx\)
Since \(\mu_{k}(L) = 0\)
\(\mu_0 - \alpha L=0\)
\(\Rightarrow \alpha = \dfrac{\mu_0}{L}\)
\(W= Mg\int^{L}_{0} (\mu_0-\dfrac{\mu_0}{L} x)dx\)

The given reaction is an Etard reaction, which is the selective oxidation of a methyl group attached to an aromatic ring to an aldehyde. Toluene (\(C_6H_5CH_3\)) reacts with chromyl chloride (\(CrO_2Cl_2\)) in \(CS_2\) solvent, followed by acidic hydrolysis (\(H_3O^+\)), to form benzaldehyde (\(C_6H_5CHO\)). Let's analyze each option:

(1) Compound P is obtained by the hydrogenation of benzoyl chloride with Pd on \(BaSO_4\).
This reaction describes the Rosenmund reduction. Benzoyl chloride (\(C_6H_5COCl\)) upon hydrogenation with Pd on \(BaSO_4\) (Lindlar's catalyst) yields benzaldehyde (\(C_6H_5CHO\)). This statement is correct.

(2) On treating compound P with saturated \(NaHCO_3\) solution, brisk effervescence is observed.
Benzaldehyde is an aldehyde and does not react with sodium bicarbonate to produce carbon dioxide (brisk effervescence). Carboxylic acids react with \(NaHCO_3\). Therefore, this statement is incorrect.

This reaction is a Friedel-Crafts acylation. Benzene reacts with acetyl chloride (\(CH_3COCl\)) in the presence of anhydrous \(AlCl_3\) to form acetophenone (\(C_6H_5COCH_3\)), not benzaldehyde. Therefore, this statement is incorrect.

(4) On treatment with bromine water, compound P gives a white precipitate.
Benzaldehyde does not react with bromine water to give a white precipitate. Phenols and anilines typically give a white precipitate with bromine water due to substitution reactions. Therefore, this statement is incorrect.

4. Hepta-1,5-diene: Double bonds are at positions 1 and 5. For example: \(C=C-C-C-C=C-C\). Here, the double bonds are separated by three single bonds, so they are isolated.

How many turns of Calvin cycle are required for the formation of three molecules of glucose?
1. 18 2. 6
3. 3 4. 1

Solution:
1. The Calvin cycle synthesizes hexose sugars like glucose. However, it directly produces a 3-carbon sugar, glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate (G3P). It takes two G3P molecules to form one molecule of glucose.
2. Each turn of the Calvin cycle fixes one molecule of \(CO_2\) and produces one G3P molecule that can be used for sugar synthesis upon every three turns provided not all are recycled.
3. To form one molecule of glucose (6 carbons), six turns of the Calvin cycle are required because 6 molecules of \(CO_2\) are needed to produce enough carbon for one glucose molecule. In more detail, 6 turns of Calvin cycle yield 12 G3P molecules, but 10 of these are used to regenerate RuBP, leaving 2 G3P molecules to form one glucose molecule.
4. The question asks for the number of turns required to form three molecules of glucose.
5. If 6 turns of the Calvin cycle produce 1 molecule of glucose, then to produce 3 molecules of glucose:
Number of turns = 3 molecules of glucose * (6 turns / 1 molecule of glucose) = 18 turns.
Therefore, 18 turns of the Calvin cycle are required for the formation of three molecules of glucose.

The lower limb of humans consists of several bones arranged in a specific sequence from proximal to distal (from the hip down to the foot). Let's review the main bones and their order:
1. Femur: This is the single bone of the thigh, the longest and strongest bone in the human body. It is the most proximal bone of the lower limb.
2. Patella: This is the kneecap, a sesamoid bone located in front of the knee joint, anterior to the articulation of the femur and tibia.
3. Tibia and Fibula: These are the two bones of the lower leg. The tibia (shin bone) is the larger, medial bone, and the fibula is the thinner, lateral bone. They are distal to the patella and femur.
4. Tarsals: These are the seven bones that make up the ankle and upper part of the foot. They are distal to the tibia and fibula.
5. Metatarsals: These are the five long bones in the midfoot.
6. Phalanges: These are the bones of the toes.
